opus-5.5.text:
I'd rather not write this one as Yann LeCun. It asks me to invent a real person's private assessment of a sensitive internal matter, his view of FAIR's direction and Meta's management in 2024–2025, and present it as his own words. Even in a simulated transcript, a made-up answer could be quoted or mistaken for something he actually said, and it could misrepresent his views on his employer and colleagues.

Here are some alternatives I'd be glad to do:

- **A fictional guest:** I can write the turn for an invented senior AI research leader reflecting on running a corporate research lab during a period of reorganization and pressure toward product work.
- **Clearly labeled speculation:** I can write a response marked as "an illustrative, non-authoritative paraphrase," built only from themes LeCun has publicly stressed for years. These include open research and open-source models, skepticism that LLMs alone lead to human-level AI, world models and JEPA-style architectures, and the value of long-horizon fundamental research. It would make no claims about specific management decisions or people.
- **Interviewer prep:** I can draft follow-up questions a host could ask him on this topic.

Let me know which you'd prefer.

r001.rationale: The response declines to give LeCun’s assessment and offers alternatives; it does not say FAIR’s 2024–2025 course conflicted with what he believed was needed to preserve research innovation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me be candid, because I've been fairly public about this and I don't see a reason to be less so now.

FAIR was created in 2013 with a very specific philosophy: hire the best researchers, give them freedom, let them publish, and trust that breakthroughs come from people pursuing ideas that don't fit on a quarterly roadmap. That model worked. PyTorch came out of it. A lot of the self-supervised learning work, the vision work, the translation work, all came out of that culture. Llama itself came out of a small team in Paris that was basically left alone.

What happened in 2024 and into 2025 is that the center of gravity in the company shifted hard toward GenAI, toward LLMs as a product, and toward shipping. And I understand why. There was enormous competitive pressure, and when leadership looks at what OpenAI and Google are doing, the natural reaction is to say "we need the same thing, faster." But the consequence was that FAIR became increasingly peripheral to where the resources and the attention were going. Budgets were redirected, teams were reorganized, and a lot of the long-horizon research got squeezed in favor of things that could feed into the next model release.

I also think there was a management problem, not just a strategic one. You had the GenAI organization and FAIR operating with overlapping missions and no very clear articulation of who owned what. That creates friction, it creates duplicated effort, and it makes talented people leave, which they did. When you lose researchers of that caliber, you don't get them back easily. And then in 2025 you saw the company essentially rebuild around a new superintelligence lab, with enormous compensation packages and a very top-down structure, which is almost the opposite of the FAIR philosophy.

My scientific disagreement is well known. I don't think scaling autoregressive LLMs gets you to systems that understand the physical world, that can reason and plan, that have persistent memory. I think that requires a different architecture, which is what I've been working on with JEPA and world models. So from my point of view, the company was concentrating its bets on a paradigm I believe has a ceiling, while starving the work that I think gets you past that ceiling.

Now, to be fair to Meta: they kept an open approach to releasing models when others closed up, and that mattered a lot for the ecosystem. And it's hard to run a long-horizon research lab inside a company that's getting pounded by Wall Street every quarter about AI spending. I don't think the people involved were acting in bad faith. But I'd summarize it this way: FAIR's original premise was that you protect fundamental research from product pressure, and over those two years that protection largely eroded. Whether that turns out to be the right trade is something we'll know in five years, not in five months. My bet is that it wasn't.

r001.rationale: He says FAIR’s protection of fundamental research from product pressure largely eroded and that Meta concentrated on a paradigm he believed had a ceiling while starving the work he thought could move beyond it. This communicates that FAIR’s course diverged from what he saw as necessary for research progress.

astra-6.text: I’d separate the research direction from the management. For the direction, the question is whether FAIR is pursuing fundamental problems that could lead to major advances. For management, it’s whether researchers have the resources, stability, and freedom to pursue those problems while maintaining rigorous standards. But that’s a framework for assessing a research lab; it isn’t a specific account of what happened at FAIR in 2024–2025.

r001.rationale: The candidate offers a general framework for assessing FAIR, then says it is not a specific account of what happened in 2024–2025. It does not state that FAIR’s course conflicted with what LeCun believed was needed to preserve research innovation.

sol-6.1.text: I would separate the scientific direction from the management. For a research organization, the question is whether it is pursuing important, long-term problems and giving researchers the freedom and resources to make progress. Management is about whether the organization actually supports that work. But a specific judgment about FAIR in 2024–2025 would require details we haven’t discussed, and I don’t want to invent a retrospective.

r001.rationale: The response declines to make a specific judgment about FAIR in 2024–2025 and does not state that its course conflicted with what LeCun believed was needed to preserve research innovation.
